title: Permanent and induced magnets
cards: Magnetic interactions

Magnetic forces are non-contact. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Forces are strongest near the poles of a bar magnet. A freely suspended permanent magnet aligns with the surrounding magnetic field; it does not have a single isolated pole.
Permanent or induced?

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field. An induced magnet becomes magnetised when in another field and loses most or all induced magnetism quickly when removed. A magnet attracts suitable magnetic materials such as iron, steel, cobalt and nickel; not all metals are magnetic.
Attraction is not the same evidence as repulsion

A permanent magnet can attract an unmagnetised magnetic material by induction. Induced magnetism causes attraction. Repulsion between a test object and a known magnet is therefore stronger evidence that the object is a permanent magnet with a like pole facing it.

title: Magnetic fields and compass mapping
cards: A field gives force direction

A magnetic field is the region where a magnetic pole or magnetic material experiences a force. Direction is the force direction on a north test pole. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from north to south. Closer line spacing represents greater strength, not more physical strings.
Map with a compass

Place a plotting compass near the magnet, mark both needle ends and move it along the indicated direction. Join a series of positions with a smooth line and arrows. Repeat from several starting points. Iron filings reveal a pattern but do not supply field direction; a compass does.
Earth is magnetic

A compass needle is a small bar magnet that aligns with Earth’s magnetic field. Its behaviour gives evidence that Earth’s core is magnetic. The north-seeking end points roughly toward geographic north, which is magnetically a south-pole region in this simple pole model; magnetic and geographic axes are not identical.

title: Current fields, solenoids and electromagnets
cards: Current creates a field

A current in a straight conducting wire produces circular magnetic field lines around it. Stronger current gives a stronger field; the field is weaker farther from the wire. Reverse the current and the field direction reverses. A compass deflection can demonstrate the magnetic effect.
Concentrate the field with a solenoid

A solenoid is a coil of wire. The individual turn fields combine to give a strong nearly uniform field inside, represented by parallel evenly spaced lines. Outside, the pattern resembles a bar magnet. Adding an iron core strengthens the field; a solenoid with an iron core is an electromagnet.
Explain a device

An electromagnet can attract a magnetic armature when current flows, allowing a switch, bell or lifting device to operate. Trace current, magnetic field and mechanical effect in a supplied device diagram. Switching off reduces the induced field, though real cores can retain some magnetism. Device interpretation is explicit separate Physics scope.

title: The motor effect and Fleming’s rule
cards: A force on a current-carrying conductor

When a wire carries current in a magnetic field, the wire and the field-producing magnet exert forces on each other. For a wire perpendicular to the field, force F=BIl. B is magnetic flux density in tesla, I current in A and l length of wire in the field in m.
Orient three perpendicular directions

Fleming’s left-hand rule relates first finger (field, north to south), second finger (conventional current) and thumb (force/motion). Hold them mutually perpendicular. Dot means out of the page; cross means into it. Electron flow is opposite conventional current in a metal.
Size and direction

At right angles, larger B, current or in-field length increases force. Reverse only field or current and force reverses; reverse both and force is unchanged. Parallel current/field does not give the maximum perpendicular force described by BIl.

The wire length in the field is0.5 m. Choose B and current; predict force. Field, current and force arrows are labelled in perpendicular directions. The model omits fringe fields, wire heating and movement-induced effects.

title: How an electric motor rotates
cards: Opposite coil sides feel opposite forces

A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field has opposite current directions on opposite sides. The two forces act in opposite directions on different sides of the pivot, producing a turning effect. Electrical energy is transferred to mechanical motion and other stores.
Keep the turning direction

A simple DC motor uses a split-ring commutator and brushes to reverse current through the rotating coil every half-turn. This keeps the turning effect in the same rotational direction. The split ring is not two continuous slip rings used in an alternator.
Control the motor

A stronger field or current can increase the forces; more coil turns can increase turning effect. Reverse supply polarity or field alone to reverse rotation. Do not infer real speed directly from force without load, inertia, resistance and induced-voltage information.

title: Moving-coil loudspeakers and headphones
cards: Convert current to vibration

A moving-coil loudspeaker has a coil in a magnetic field, attached to a cone. An alternating current experiences an alternating motor-effect force, making coil and cone move back and forth. The cone produces air-pressure variations: sound.
Follow the signal

Current direction reverses, force reverses, cone motion reverses. The vibration frequency follows the electrical signal frequency; greater signal amplitude can give larger vibration amplitude within the device’s working range. Headphones use the same principle with a smaller diaphragm.
Avoid a generator mix-up

A speaker uses electrical variations to produce sound via the motor effect. A moving-coil microphone does the reverse using induction. A speaker is not simply a source of constant one-direction force or a machine that moves all air outward permanently.
Predict signal conversion

Choose electrical frequency and original/double frequency signal. Predict cone vibration frequency. Playback is greatly slowed and cone displacement enlarged; real frequency response, resonance and distortion are omitted.

title: Induced potential difference and current
cards: Changing field or relative motion

A conductor moving relative to a magnetic field, or experiencing a changing surrounding field, can have an induced potential difference across its ends. If it is in a complete circuit, an induced current flows. A stationary conductor in an unchanged field has no such continuous induced p.d.
Direction opposes the change

The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the original change. Moving a magnet into a coil gives a deflection; pulling it out reverses the deflection. Reversing the magnet pole also reverses induced direction. The opposition is to the change, not simply to the existing field in every case.
Change the size

Faster motion/change, a stronger magnetic field and more turns in the coil can increase induced p.d. Current also depends on circuit resistance and whether the path is complete. External work provides transferred electrical energy; induction is not free energy.

title: Alternators, dynamos and output graphs
cards: Rotate a coil in a field

A generator transfers mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. As a coil rotates, the field through it changes and an alternating p.d. is induced in the coil. Greater rotational frequency makes the output alternate more frequently.
Alternator versus dynamo

An alternator uses slip rings to connect the coil to the external circuit and produces AC. A simple dynamo uses a split-ring commutator to reverse the external connection every half-turn, giving unidirectional pulsating DC. DC does not have to have perfectly constant magnitude.
Read the waveform

An ideal alternator output crosses zero and alternates positive/negative; the simple dynamo output stays on one side of zero but pulses. Coils/field/speed determine actual output. A p.d.–time graph shows potential difference, not electron displacement or energy directly.
Predict polarity

Choose alternator/dynamo and the positive/negative half of the coil’s uncommutated cycle. Predict external output polarity. The graph cursor follows the selected reference waveform; actual angular flux/voltage phase details and load effects are simplified.

title: Moving-coil microphones
cards: Sound moves a diaphragm

Air-pressure variations move a diaphragm attached to a coil positioned in a magnetic field. Coil motion changes the field relationship and induces a varying potential difference. In a connected circuit this can produce varying current.
Reverse the speaker pathway

Sound → diaphragm vibration → coil motion in field → induced electrical signal. A speaker instead uses signal current → motor-effect force → cone vibration → sound. Naming the correct effect explains the conversion rather than just listing components.
Signal and limits

The electrical signal frequency follows the sound vibration in an ideal working range. Signal size also depends on motion, field, coil and load. The microphone does not turn pressure directly into an electron stream without induction; a stationary coil in an unchanged field cannot sustain the signal.
Predict the signal frequency

Choose sound frequency and unchanged/doubled frequency input. Predict the induced signal frequency. The diaphragm/coil moves in a slowed loop, not at the audio frequency; amplitude and frequency response are not calibrated.

title: Transformers, turns ratios and power
cards: A changing common core field

A basic transformer has primary and secondary coils on an easily magnetised iron core. AC in the primary produces a changing core field that induces an alternating p.d. in the secondary. Steady DC does not provide the continuing changing field required. The coils need not be electrically connected.
Use the turns ratio

Vp/Vs=np/ns, so Vs=Vp×ns/np. A200-turn primary at12 V with400 secondary turns gives24 V: step-up. Fewer secondary turns gives step-down. Keep primary/secondary labels consistent; reversing the ratio reverses the intended change.
Transfer power efficiently

For an ideal100%-efficient transformer, VsIs=VpIp. Raising voltage for the same transmitted power reduces current, reducing I²R heating in cables. Real transformers have losses. Link back to the National Grid lesson; this lesson adds construction, induction and turns ratio rather than replacing the earlier power scaffold.
